# Setting up {.unnumbered}

Work through this page **before Day 1**. It takes about half an hour, most of
which is waiting for downloads. Doing it in advance means Session 1 starts with
you writing model code rather than installing software.

You need four things: Julia, a code editor (we suggest VSCode), Quarto, and the course materials
themselves. Follow the sections in order.

::: {.callout-tip}
## If you get stuck, try to keep installing the rest of the software and make a note of where you got stuck. 

A setup problem that has cost you thirty minutes alone could be a ten-minute fix in
person. Note where you got stuck and move on. We will help you fix it on Day 1 if you can't get it working.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Never used a terminal? Start here

A terminal is a text-based window where you type commands to control your
computer. Instead of clicking folders and icons with a mouse, you use your
keyboard to tell the system what to do. Where a step below says "run this in a
terminal", the grey box beneath it is the line to paste in, one line at a time,
each followed by `Enter`.

To open one:

- **macOS**: press `Cmd`+`Space`, type `Terminal`, press `Enter`.
- **Windows**: click Start, type `PowerShell`, press `Enter`.
- **Linux**: your desktop's terminal application, usually `Ctrl`+`Alt`+`T`.

VSCode also has one built in, and it is the easier option once you reach
[step 2](#install-vscode-and-the-julia-extension): open it with *Terminal* →
*New Terminal*. It starts in whichever folder you have open, which is what steps
5 and 6 need. If you would rather not go hunting for a terminal application at
all, do step 2 first and then come back here.
:::

## 1. Install Julia

Install Julia through **juliaup**, a small tool that manages Julia versions for
you. It means you can update Julia later, or hold several versions side by side,
without reinstalling anything.

On **Windows**, you can do this without a terminal. Open the **Microsoft Store**
app, search for **Julia**, and click *Get*. That installs juliaup, and there is
nothing else to click. The
[store listing](https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9NJNWW8PVKMN) is the same
thing if you would rather follow a link. If you prefer a command, this does
exactly the same job:

```bash
winget install julia -s msstore
```

On **macOS or Linux**, there is no point-and-click equivalent, so this one line
in a terminal is the whole install:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://install.julialang.org | sh
```

It asks you to confirm where it will install things; press `Enter` to accept the
defaults.

Then close and reopen your terminal, and install the version this course is
built and tested against. These two lines are typed, on every platform including
Windows:

```bash
juliaup add 1.12
juliaup default 1.12
```

Check that it worked by typing `julia`:

```bash
$ julia
               _
   _       _ _(_)_     |  Documentation: https://docs.julialang.org
  (_)     | (_) (_)    |
   _ _   _| |_  __ _   |  Type "?" for help, "]?" for Pkg help.
  | | | | | | |/ _` |  |
  | | |_| | | | (_| |  |  Version 1.12.5
 _/ |\__'_|_|_|\__'_|  |
|__/                   |

julia>
```

Your patch version may be higher than `1.12.5`; anything starting `1.12` is
right. That prompt is the Julia **REPL**, where you will spend a good deal of
the workshop. Leave it with `exit()` or `Ctrl-D`.

If `julia` is not found, see [Julia is not found](#julia-is-not-found) below.

## 2. Install VSCode and the Julia extension

Download Visual Studio Code from
[code.visualstudio.com/download](https://code.visualstudio.com/download) and
install it.

Then install the Julia extension: open the Extensions panel with
`Cmd`+`Shift`+`X` (macOS) or `Ctrl`+`Shift`+`X` (Windows and Linux), search for
**Julia**, and click *Install*.

Restart VSCode afterwards. To confirm the extension works, open the command
palette with `Cmd`/`Ctrl`+`Shift`+`P`, run **Julia: Start REPL**, and check that
a `julia>` prompt appears in the panel at the bottom.

If the extension cannot find Julia, see
[VSCode cannot find Julia](#vscode-cannot-find-julia) below.

## 3. Install Quarto

The chapters and worksheets are Quarto documents. You need both the Quarto
program and its VSCode extension: the extension is what runs a single code cell
while you read, and the program is what turns a finished worksheet into an HTML
report.

1. Download and install Quarto 1.9 or newer from
   [quarto.org/docs/get-started](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/).
2. In VSCode, install the **Quarto** extension the same way you installed the Julia one.

Confirm the program is on your path:

```bash
quarto --version
```

## 4. Get the course materials

If you use **git**:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/epirecipes/modeling-epidemics-julia.git
cd modeling-epidemics-julia
```

If you do not use git, open
[the repository](https://github.com/epirecipes/modeling-epidemics-julia), choose
*Code* then *Download ZIP*, and unzip it somewhere you can find again.

Then open that folder in VSCode with *File* → *Open Folder*. Open the folder
itself (e.g., `modeling-epidemics-julia-main`), not an individual file. Julia and Quarto both need to know which
project you are working in, and VSCode tells them by which folder is open. Be sure you are opening the specific project folder, rather than your general `Downloads` folder.

## 5. Install the course packages

From the top of the folder you just opened, run:

```bash
julia --project=. -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()'
```

This downloads every package the course uses, at the exact versions it was
tested with. It is the longest step — expect ten to twenty minutes on a good
connection, and do it before you travel rather than on workshop wifi.

::: {.callout-note}
## What `--project=.` means

It tells Julia to use the set of packages declared in this folder. Almost every
Julia command in this course carries it. If you forget it, Julia falls back to
your personal default set, the course packages are not there, and `using
CairoMakie` fails — which is the single most common problem people hit. See
[a package seems to be missing](#a-package-seems-to-be-missing).
:::

## 6. Check that it worked

Run this from the top of the folder. It loads the two packages the first
worksheet needs and builds a figure.

```bash
julia --project=. -e '
using CairoMakie, StableRNGs
println("Julia version: ", VERSION)
fig = Figure(size = (400, 300))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1])
xs = 0:0.05:6
lines!(ax, xs, exp.(-xs))
println("CairoMakie and StableRNGs load, and a figure builds.")
println("Setup complete.")'
```

You should see the Julia version, then the two confirmation lines.

**The first run will be slow** — a minute or more, possibly several. Julia
compiles code the first time it is used, and the plotting stack is large. This
is not a hang, and it is exactly why it is worth running now rather than in
Session 1: the compiled result is cached, so the same code is fast for the rest
of the workshop.

Once this passes, you are ready. Everything below is either troubleshooting or
optional.

## 7. Running code while you follow along

You will meet the course material in three forms, and each is run differently.
It is worth trying all three now, on any file, so that none of it is new during
a session.

**Worksheets and chapters** are Quarto documents, made of prose with code cells.
Put the cursor inside a cell and press `Ctrl`+`Shift`+`Enter` to run that cell.
Output appears below it. This is how you will work through the sessions.

To turn a finished worksheet into an HTML report, run every cell top to bottom
in a fresh session from a terminal:

```bash
quarto render worksheets/prerequisites/01-julia-essentials.qmd
```

**Your own scripts** are plain `.jl` files. Put the cursor on a line and press
`Shift`+`Enter` to send just that line to the REPL. To run several lines
together, fence them between `#%%` markers and press `Alt`+`Enter` anywhere
inside:

```julia
#%%
u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]
p  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
#%%
```

Because `#` starts a comment in Julia, you can label a block by writing after
the marker — `#%% force of infection` — and the file still runs as an ordinary
script.

**The REPL itself** is for short questions: what a function takes, whether a
package is installed, what a value is. It has three modes beyond the ordinary
`julia>` prompt. Type the character at an empty prompt to enter one, and
`Backspace` to leave:

| Key | Mode | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `?` | help | you want a function's arguments — `?expm1` |
| `]` | package | a package seems missing — `]st` also names the active project |
| `;` | shell | you need `ls` or `git status` without leaving Julia |

## If something goes wrong

### Julia is not found

Your shell does not know where Julia was installed. On macOS or Linux, add
juliaup's directory to your path by putting this line in `~/.zshrc` (or
`~/.bashrc` if you use bash — `echo $SHELL` tells you which):

```bash
export PATH="$HOME/.juliaup/bin:$PATH"
```

Open a new terminal afterwards. On Windows, the usual cause is that the shell
was open while Julia was installed, so close it and open a new one.

### VSCode cannot find Julia

If `julia` works in a terminal but VSCode reports that it cannot find it, tell
the extension where to look. First get the path:

```bash
which julia     # macOS and Linux
where julia     # Windows
```

Then open VSCode's settings with `Cmd`/`Ctrl`+`,`, search for **Julia
Executable Path**, and paste the result in.

### A package seems to be missing

If `using CairoMakie` fails with a message about the package not being found,
Julia is almost certainly running outside the course project.

Check which project is active: at the Julia prompt, press `]` to enter package
mode. The prompt changes to show the active project's name, which should be
`(EpiModelingCourse)`. If it shows `(@v1.12)` instead, you are in your personal
default environment. Press `Backspace` to leave package mode, quit with
`exit()`, and start Julia again with `--project=.` from the top of the course
folder.

### A cell runs forever the first time

That is compilation, not a hang — see [step 6](#check-that-it-worked). It
happens once per session, per package.

## Optional extras

**A font that renders Greek letters.** The course writes parameters as `β`, `γ`
and `λ` so the code matches the equations. Most fonts show these, but
[JuliaMono](https://juliamono.netlify.app/) is designed for Julia and covers
every symbol the course uses. Install it, then set VSCode's *Editor: Font
Family* to `JuliaMono`.

**Typing Greek letters.** You do not need that font to type them. At any Julia
prompt, and in `.jl` files, type a backslash, the name, then `Tab`:
`\beta`+`Tab` gives `β`. Inside a Quarto `.qmd` file, which is where you will
write every worksheet cell, that completion often does not fire.

For those, install the **Unicode Latex** extension: open the Extensions panel,
search for `unicode-latex`, and install the one published by *Omer Sheikh*. Its
symbol names are generated from Julia's own REPL completions, so they are the
names this course uses. To insert a character, open the command palette with
`Cmd`/`Ctrl`+`Shift`+`P`, type `unicode`, choose **Unicode: Insert Math
Symbol**, type the symbol's name, and press `Enter`. Nothing has to be
configured per symbol.

Every worksheet also opens with a table of the symbols it uses, ready to copy.

**The interactive notebooks.** Every unit also comes as a Pluto notebook with
sliders, linked at the end of its chapter and, for the taught sessions, on the
[workshop resources](resources.qmd) page. Step 5 already installed Pluto, so
starting it is one line:

```bash
julia --project=. -e 'using Pluto; Pluto.run()'
```

It opens in your browser. Use *Open a notebook* and give it a path such as
`notebooks/chapters/01-foundations.jl`.

A Pluto notebook is not a script that runs top to bottom. Its cells form a
network: change one, and every cell that depends on it re-runs by itself. That
is what keeps the sliders honest, and it is why cell order on the page does not
have to match the order things happen in.

**A second package set, for self-study only.** One unit, parameter estimation,
needs a package that conflicts with the rest of the course, so it has an
environment of its own. It is **not** taught in the workshop, so skip this
unless and until you work through that chapter yourself:

```bash
julia --project=environments/ch08 -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()'
```
